utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would like to briefly deal with the exhibit list, Mr. Lukic. I think we have now the exhibit list of the 9th of July. And on that list, let me start with D01099, the number provisionally assigned. So that's number 6 on the first page. It says that there is no English translation, but I do understand it has been uploaded now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You therefore tender it. Any objections, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D01099 is admitted. Next one, D01100, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections to any of them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D01100 admitted. D1101, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. D1102.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. D1103.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. D1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. D1105. It seems that a wrong English translation is uploaded. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not aware that it was corrected yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Therefore, the number assigned remains provisionally assigned to that number. For D1106, there is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what would you like us to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MFI it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MFI. D1106 is MFI'd. Then, finally, D1107.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Now the first five, I think, let me see. D -- I have to look at those. Some of them were MFI'd pending translations. I think for D1094, it's a bit unclear where we stand there, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have D numbers on this list. If you can give me 1D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 32617.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I have on this list no 1D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it's D1094.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is already admitted. Then let me see. Then we have 1095 which is MFI'd; 1096 which is also MFI'd; 1097, permission was granted to add it to the 65 ter list and is admitted; and D1098 is MFI'd. Therefore, I think we dealt with all of them until now. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we have our witness with us, we checked this D1098 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and it was MFI'd because I proposed it, to have it MFI'd. But this morning we checked, the English translation is complete and already uploaded as complete. So it was my mistake actually when I said that the English translation is not complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So D1098, which was MFI'd, and is 1D05388 is ready to be admitted. Any objections, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1098 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misic. Mr. Misic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Misic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, during your direct testimony in this case, you were shown the Srebrenica missing reports, P1901, that was prepared by Helga Brunborg. Now, I take it that you did not study this report in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in preparing for your testimony, I take it you didn't study any other reports relating to missing persons that had been prepared by other expert witnesses in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: On that basis, is it therefore fair to say that you don't know the extent to which experts in this case may or may not have relied on any information provided by the Missing Persons Institute?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were asked about missing persons certificates that were sent to the Tribunal from the Missing Persons Institute, and you looked at one such certificate and you stated as follows: "I'm not going to speak about the content of the certificate whether it is correct or not but it is illegal ..." Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And would this comment apply equally to any other missing persons certificates that were sent to the Tribunal as part of the same batch?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If they had not passed through the normal procedure, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I take it that you've not reviewed any of the 193 certificates that are referenced in the so-called POD annex which relates to non-Srebrenica missing, in this case P2797; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the same document -- the certificate, can I have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number to start with, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The number was the POD annex P2797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2797. Perhaps we have a look at it. The witness asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sure. And it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document references 193 missing persons certificates that were provided by the Missing Persons Institute, and my question was whether you had reviewed any of these 193 missing persons certificates.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning these certificates, I asked the chief of sector in charge to give his opinion. Since he did not say that he would stand by them, although they were done by the sector, I didn't go into it any further because in my eyes they were a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is you didn't review them? Is that the short answer to the question? The question was whether you did review any of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the sample. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you say "the sample," that's the one certificate we looked at yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now one question. You said the chief of the sector "did not say that he would stand by them, although they were done by the sector." And you said: "I didn't go into it any further because in my eyes they were a forgery." Now, a forgery can be two things: Either the document comes from where it says it comes but the content is not accurate; or a forgery can be that a document is not what it looks like. It does not come from the authority or the institute it claims it comes from. What kind of forgery were you referring to? That's one. And then the second question is what made them in your eyes a forgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, because the chief of sector takes his distance from this document, and he was the one who was competent for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chief Simanovic -- is Simanovic [as interpreted] is supposed to stand by this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not -- you told us that. That's not an answer to my question. You said he didn't stand by that and in your eyes it was a forgery. I asked you about forgery. What kind of forgery is it? Is it content not accurate; or is it that it's just a fraud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the way it was created and because the institute is unable to stand by their document. The stamp of the institute should never have been affixed on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, to be clear, it's the process by which those documents were provided that you are concerned with, but you've no idea of the actual content of that document and whether or not that content is accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content, in my opinion, is most probably not correct. And I say that because it has not been checked by a competent official, the only person who could verify this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not interested in whether it's probably not accurate and your reasoning for it - that is, that it has not been checked by the right person - is in itself not a reason to assume that it's either correct or incorrect, and I'm referring now to the content. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. Now as regards Srebrenica-related missing person material, yesterday you indicated that of the 10.000 or 10.100, 10.200 or so missing persons records that you say were not properly verified by the Missing Persons Institute, you said that the majority of those records relate to persons linked to Srebrenica events in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that the Srebrenica missing reports, P1901, does not rely on any missing person information provided by the Missing Persons Institute, whether verified or not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now during your testimony, you were shown a collection of documents in Exhibit D1098. And these were the collection of documents -- missing persons-related documents that related to 17 different persons, all of whom appear to be connected to Srebrenica. Now, only 8 of these 17 are actually referred to in the Srebrenica missing report in this case, P1909, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just on this point, you've indicated that you'll take a look at this entire exhibit which relates to the 17 persons. Now, if it assists, I can provide you, perhaps after the testimony of the witness, with the eight persons who are actually included in the Srebrenica missing persons report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at those portions, the witness has not specifically given evidence upon, Mr. Lukic and Mr. Jeremy, both of you, if you could give very brief explanations as what, Mr. Lukic, you would wish us to look at in relation to those, where apparently you consider there to be inconsistencies. And if you, Mr. Jeremy, again would give, again, not full argument, but just point at relevant things we should just look at. That would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, during your testimony you also referred to missing persons information that was obtained by the ICMP, and ICMP documentation form part of some of the exhibits that we looked at. Now, missing person information is not used as a source of missing person information by Prosecution experts in this case. Were you aware of that? I should say missing persons information provided by the ICMP is not used as a source for missing persons information by experts in this case and whether you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your evidence, we've looked at many different sources of information relating to missing persons from the ICRC, the ICMP, the Federal Commission on Missing and Exhumed Persons. We've looked at birth certificates, we've looked at death certificates, and even a military monograph. Now, I take it that we can agree that you've got no idea of the sources that the experts in this case relied on in preparing their conclusions relating to missing persons?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, similarly, you've no idea of the methodology that was employed by those experts in arriving at their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to conclude by looking at a specific example and one that we've looked at in -- you looked at with Mr. Lukic in the recent days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll need to go into private session, please, to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, this Chamber has received evidence, that's P1481, page 7, that this Snagovo grave-site area refers to a general area in which multiple secondary mass graves were located, graves that were linked to a primary mass grave in Orahovac, and that's P1737. Sir, are you aware of this connection between these graves?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly but I do know something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know that Snagovo is in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now could we please go to D1096, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, coming up on the screen is a document that you looked at with Mr. Lukic yesterday and the day before. So, sir, you'll recognise on the document on the screen before you. This is an ICRC --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- information request, and we've already looked at the information in recent days. We see the same name that we just looked at, the same personal details, and we see the date of this certificate is the -- May the 23rd, 1996. Now, just focusing for a moment on the form rather than the substance of this document, you've looked at a number of other ICRC information requests in recent days. Now, the Chamber has received evidence, and that's page 37 of P1900, that ICRC data is systematically updated and reviewed and closed cases - for example, confirmed dead or alive - are excluded on an ongoing basis. I take it that you are aware of this systemic update and review process carried out by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page please in this document. Actually, let's skip forward to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see on the screen before us a DNA report. It's from the ICRC. We see -- sorry, ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see in the top right corner a reference to a protocol number, and that's the name number that we looked at in the document that we had on the screen before this document, P1901. Sir, we see that the site's location is Snagovo, so it's the same location. And we see the possible identity name, which I won't read out, but we see it's the same name. We see the reference to donors, and we see three names. Then we see the reference to the DNA profile from a listed bone. And below that, we see the -- we read that the DNA profile from a bone was matched to a family or family blood samples, and we see the probability of relatedness at 99.99. And it goes on. And lastly we see that this document is dated the 9th of March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could just go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And again we see identical information in terms of the site location, the protocol number, the possible identity, and the donors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Here the DNA profile from the obtained listed bone has a different code. So, sir, this would suggest that this is a different bone sample; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we also see the percentage match or the likelihood of the match and the percentage, which is a similar percentage to the one that we've just looked at, and we see that this particular document is dated the 18th of September, 2006. So, sir, on the basis of the ICRC document we've looked at and the two ICMP DNA match reports, we see that this is a person who, according to the May 23rd, 1996 ICRC record, went missing on the 11th of July, 1995 in the forest in Srebrenica; and then ten years later, we see that, according to the ICMP, two bone samples taken from this person were DNA matched to blood provided by three members of his family. Would you agree that the -- that at least the documents that we have seen indicate that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you'd agree that the ICMP documents we've looked at indicate that this individual was located in a mass grave; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the Srebrenica missing report that we looked at, P1901, is dated 2009 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jeremy. Are you going to move away from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm going to make a point related to it, but if Your Honour would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question relates to both of these two DNA certificates. I would ask that they be put side by side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see -- on the left, we see page 4 of the document in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- no, it's now been changed. To the left, we now see page 3 in e-court, and from the photograph it seems that these are two teeth which have provided the sample; whereas on the right, we see page 4 from this document in e-court, which seems to be a bone fragment rather than teeth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can I ask my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I was just trying to get everything straight on the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, during evidence in-chief it was suggested to you that the signatures on these two certificates are different. Can you have a look at them and tell us whether, indeed, they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that I said anything about signatures, but in my view these signatures are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, as regards ICMP DNA identifications. Now, the Srebrenica missing report that we looked at, P1901, was dated 2009. Now, this Chamber has received evidence - for example, P2792, page 10 - that in 2013 this information was updated to take into account the ongoing ICMP DNA identifications. And that as of 2013, 85.8 per cent of those persons listed in the 2009 Srebrenica missing list had been found in Srebrenica-related mass graves and identified by DNA. Were you aware of that percentage of DNA identification of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, in this -- in the context of these DNA identifications and the process that goes behind them, which I know that you are aware of, in respect to this particular individual referred to and the documents that we are looking at, you challenged the accuracy of the missing person information and the DNA identification by offering a document, a monograph of a unit in the ABiH, which refers to an individual with similar personal details but with a different date of birth. That's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at a single moment did I dispute the ICMP findings as far as identification was concerned. The only thing I'm challenging is the ICMP list regarding the circumstances of death. What is in dispute with regard to this person is the place of death and the circumstances of death. Not verification. So I'm saying that all lists, whatever they may be, have to undergo a process of verification. So I'm not challenging the identification of this person or the findings of the ICMP as regards identification. And it's not only that I'm speaking about this case but in general as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, as I understand it, you believe that the circumstances of death relating to this individual are -- according to the monograph of the ABiH, you believe that this individual died in December 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you challenge whether that this individual was indeed found in the Snagovo mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see any logic in that; namely, that an individual that lost his life due to an unfortunate accident can find a place in a mass grave and the death occurred after the war. And I don't think it would be justified for that kind of person to be buried in a mass grave in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the sentence before the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat the final two sentences of your answer for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the person lost his life after the war. The person was killed by his own forces, his own unit. He was found on the spot. Now, where is the logic there? How can that person have the status of a missing person, and how can that person be found in a mass grave? I don't see any reason for that and I don't see any logic in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, if I understood your previous answer, you were not challenging the ICMP identification, so I understood that you weren't challenging the fact that this person was found in the Snagovo mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But you challenge the circumstances in which this individual was placed into the Snagovo mass grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may just for a second. I don't think that Mr. Misic speaks, but if you clarify. There was some translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- you want to clarify something now, or would you like the witness to further answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that if he can take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it a problem with the question or is it a problem with the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Answer was actually given in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand the English language? Could you please first answer my question. Do you understand the English language? Not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. English, I don't understand. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question posed by my learned friend on page 18, line 20, was actually, in my opinion, and how I heard it was answered after the first part of the question. So I would kindly ask Mr. Jeremy to ask questions separately. We have two questions in this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please the -- your understanding of what was challenged and what was not challenged, could you revisit that, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness put his earphones on again. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, do you dispute that this individual was found in the Snagovo mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again. There is no base that we are not challenging until the opposite is proven. Every base can be this or that, so the circumstances of death and the time of death are something that we have to establish in the process of verification as a commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not -- I think the simple -- let's start taking it one by one. Do you dispute that the teeth and the bone that was examined, DNA examined by the ICMP, do you challenge that they were found in the Snagovo grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not challenging that they were found -- well, I'm not going to challenge it. But what is questionable is on the basis of circumstances of death, how can they be in Snagovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that later. So you do not challenge that those body parts, which were DNA tested, were found in Snagovo. You do not dispute that. Second question is do you dispute the DNA testing and its result as done by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, on that basis, therefore, if, according to the ABiH monologue, this individual died in December 1995 in Kladanj, then according to you how did he find himself or how did he get to a mass grave in Snagovo in RS territory?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. So my question is: How did this individual go from Kladanj in ABiH territory in December 1995 to Snagovo in RS -- into a mass grave in Snagovo in RS territory? How would you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I've been denying. ICMP is basically a laboratory, and this information about where they were found, they get that from the pathologist or from some other person that attended exhumations at mass graves. It wasn't the ICMP that found this person. They received the bone samples from the location where they were found, from the appropriate officials, so probably the ICMP cannot stand by that. And where I do not see the link is the link between the mass grave and this person. That is what I've been challenging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I earlier asked you whether you challenged that the body parts - that is, teeth and a piece of bone - whether you challenged that they were found in the Snagovo grave. You said you didn't challenge that, but I now understand that you do challenge and that you say there must have been a mistake in saying that those body parts were found in the Snagovo grave before they arrived at the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot deny it, I cannot confirm it, that these bones were found there. I can believe that these tiny pieces of bone were found in that mass grave, but I don't see the logic. I don't see the reason. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are insisting again and again on the logic of the whole thing. Are you aware that the basis of your criticism on the logic, the basis for it is that you take it for a fact, not to be challenged, undisputed, that this person died in December in 1995 in Kladanj? As soon as you would start making that a question as well, suddenly the logical question would be a different one; that is, how to reconcile the one information with the other. And then you have to consider which of the information may be right or wrong and that would, something you've excluded until now, that would also put questions to the accuracy of the report of this person dieing in December 1995 in Kladanj. I hope you understand my short observation in relation to your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in a previous answer you've said that: "It wasn't the ICMP that found this person, they received the bone samples from the location where they were found from the appropriate officials, so probably the ICMP cannot stand by that." So are you suggesting that the process has in some way been corrupted, that bone samples and teeth were planted by somebody in the Snagovo mass grave; is that your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It is possible that there are errors. This entire example shows that the process of verification is a very complex issue, and this is an example: To the effect that not a single list can be absolutely correct until it's gone through the entire process of verification as I've already described. This is a contested issue. I can deny all of this, I can confirm all of this, conditionally speaking. You see, it is not impossible that in some way these bones reached this location. But at any rate, this person should not be linked at all as a person to the mass grave that we've been discussing, and now it is not possible to verify the circumstances that this person went missing as is stated in that document from July 1995. That is what is in dispute and that is what I've been challenging. That is what I've been trying to say. Verification is a very complex problem and it cannot be carried out only on the basis of a single document, regardless of whether it comes from the ICMP or any other institution, and that is why this has been turned into a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What makes you certain that the information about the accident in December 1995, which resulted in the death of this individual, is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That person has not been verified and that's precisely the problem I'm pointing out. The verification is very complex. Nothing has been proven or denied about this person. But considering that the verification has been done for a person with -- who is the only person with that name and surname and father's name in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, checks have been run, there is no person in Serbia whose personal data are even remotely similar. And based on this general data, we decided that person needed to be verified, and you see how many contradictions there are about the place and date of disappearance or killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have answered my question. There is no certainty at all about the death in December because it's not verified. The next question: What makes you certain that these two -- that this is the same person whose bones were identified and the person who was killed in December 1995? What makes you certain that this is really the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Checks have been run based on the records that were kept and are kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is only one such person in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With two different dates of birth; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be no two dates of birth, but it can be determined exactly based on excerpts from the register. The only disputable detail is date of birth as recorded in the monograph, but the rest is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But if there is this discrepancy with respect to the date of birth, what makes you certain that this was one and the same individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's indisputable. This person existed. An error has been identified, that error has to be corrected, and that person has to be identified. But I stress that based on all the records --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You don't answer my question. What is the evidence that this is really the same person? You say there was only one person with these names in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What is the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the checks we ran in the records; in the register of births, in the lists, in the CIPS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, for the first time you at least give indication what kind of checks were run. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, it's time for a break, I think, and we'd take a bit of a longer break. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. I'm looking at you, Mr. Lukic. What would we prefer, to finish the cross-examination in the next five minutes and then take a break of one hour or to break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, whatever fits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whatever also does not meet any objections by Mr. Mladic. Five more minutes and then?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that -- we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We continue. Mr. Jeremy, you have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we go to the next page, please, in the document that we're looking at, so the penultimate page. Sorry, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see a highlighted name in this list. And it's the same name that we have been discussing. It's the same date of birth. The disappearance in this document is actually the 12th of July, 1995. I think in some of the others we saw it was the 11th of July, 1995. Now, on these two pages is a list of 102 individuals, all of whom appear to have gone missing on the 11th or the 12th or dates close to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can scroll over to the right-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see that the grave location for all of them is Snagovo. Now, sir, if 102 individuals were found in this mass grave in Snagovo, is it your position that this individual that we were discussing was the only individual who wasn't, in fact, in that grave and somehow added into it afterwards, or do you think that more of these individuals were also in some way linked to this grave in a way that would not suggest that they were put in -- they were executed and placed into these graves?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to say anything with any certainty, because I can't. As far as the other persons are concerned, the information is probably correct, but I didn't analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did you look at any military monologues for any of these other individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you correct me, sir? Am I correct that this morning you indicated that this person died after the war in 1995? Did you use the phrase "after the war"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought. And when did the war end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, officially it was concluded with a signature in Paris in December 1995, but the peace was imposed back with the Dayton Accords in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when did the fighting stop? Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there was any fighting after the 21st of November, 1995, in any area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any area. So if this person died in December when there was no longer any fighting, what would members of the 28th Division be doing in the bush at that time? Why would there be some soldiers somewhere in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there was still smaller parts of units patrolling certain territories because there was still no confidence that the peace would last and there was still fear on all sides that some other fighting might restart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the war hadn't ended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why certain areas were controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the war hadn't ended at that time yet. If soldiers are still patrolling, then I suppose the war hasn't ended yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we have a different view of the definition of "war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Witness, we'll take a bit of a longer break as we usually do, one hour. We would like to see you back at 20 minutes to 2.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue with the re-examination of the witness, the Chamber was informed that the Defence would not be in a position to bring any witnesses immediately after the -- our recess, that is starting the 10th of August, and the Chamber wondered why, where there is still another 40 witnesses to go, at least, why there are no witnesses. The Chamber understands and has always considered any -- Christmas time, et cetera, but the Chamber does not understand why in just an ordinary week in the midst of August that no witnesses can be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the information we got from the field, and our expert witnesses were scheduled at the end of our case, and before them we would bring international witnesses. And we planned to bring those local witnesses from Balkans in August and the beginning of September, but the information we received is that nobody is available in the first week of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is not a matter about the information you receive. You should go after it yourself, as lead counsel, and take care that there are witnesses even if you have to change your schedule, even if you have to change the order of witnesses, we just can't afford to lose a whole week. You know that. We have to finish. So, therefore, if there is nothing better you report to us as that you heard from the field that in the order as you had in your mind no one would be available, the Chamber is seriously considering to count that week as time for the Defence to present its evidence, which would mean that if you don't produce it, then you lose the time. The Chamber is really seriously considering that, and a mere observation that you heard from the field that there are no witnesses is not something we would easily accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We just deemed necessary to inform the Chamber. We will try to push our witnesses to come here, even in the first week. But all we could produce were alibi witnesses, and we spoke with the Prosecution and they would not be prepared to have Srebrenica witnesses, if possible - if possible - if we were asked about it. But we are not even now, when we checked, we are not able even to bring those alibi witnesses in the first week. We will try further to contact our witnesses and we will try to fulfil it, that first week, but at the moment we do not have anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that should change. And if you need our assistance by influencing by subpoenas or whatever, the Chamber is willing to firmly support that the Defence can present its evidence, can present its witnesses, and the Chamber would regret if time would be lost in this way where it is available to the Defence to present its case. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. Mr. Lukic and I, of course, are continuing to have discussions about witnesses, but -- so it's clear, the Prosecution is absolutely ready to take on any witnesses that come, Srebrenica or otherwise. Though, as we all have done with each other, sometimes we manage to meet various courtesies, but we're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Mr. Lukic, it was just an informal announcement, which the Chamber appreciates that you have sent it, but the Chamber is now waiting for better messages. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we briefly to go to private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can. But is the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's nothing in regard of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Therefore, the witness should stay out of the courtroom until we've dealt with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, usually the usher would wait for a sign that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No -- or I can deal with that when this witness finishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll then deal with it after we've concluded hearing the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, Mr. Lukic will now re-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It will be a short re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day again, Mr. Misic. You remember the Office of the Prosecutor has put it to you that the percentage of missing persons from Republika Srpska is about 72.18 per cent, and from the Federation 74.83 per cent. In fact, this is the number of those identified.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that identified persons must also undergo the procedure of verification?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Unfortunately, we began with the verification of identified persons, which we shouldn't have done. But in any case, all missing persons -- all those who had the status of missing persons were supposed to go through the procedure of verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now briefly could we see D1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the substance of the document. Just look at the address at the top. On this document sent by a colleague of yours, we read Hamdija Cernelica street, 15/2. No, 2/15.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's our real address.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the address of Mr. Masovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Masovic is at this address too, but unfortunately he spends more time at Musala 9 Street. It's the former institute for missing persons, but not of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the one that was established first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To what address should the post arrive normally?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This address, Hamdija Cernelica 2/15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly, let's look at one document which I believe has not been tendered yet but it has been discussed. It's 65 ter 32612.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you before this page disappears, Mr. Lukic. At page 31, lines 15 to 19, you said to the witness: "You remember the Office of the Prosecutor has put to you that the percentage of missing persons from Republika Srpska is about 72.18 per cent and from Federation 74.83." Percentage of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Identified missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the word that's missing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked and you explained about the involvement or lack of involvement of your institute in the drafting of these reports. I would like to ask you this: Did ICMP keep you abreast of their actions? I mean you, as the institute.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they ranked superior to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're on this document. On our provisional transcript, page 9, line 19, the Prosecution told you that the experts of the Prosecution did not use the information provided by ICMP. Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify. As I recall, I'd said that the Prosecution didn't use missing persons-related information provided by ICMP rather than the more general information provided by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here, maybe we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you quote it literally so that we know exactly what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So page 9, line 19: "Q. Now, sir, during your testimony you also referred to a missing persons information that was obtained by the ICMP and ICMP documentation form part of some of the exhibits that we looked at. Now, missing person information is not used as a source of missing person information by Prosecution experts in this case. Were you aware of that? "I should say missing persons information provided by the ICMP is not used as a source for missing persons information by experts in this case and whether you were aware of that." Now, if we can see page 4 from the document on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do agree with Mr. Jeremy's position, that he's only referring to missing persons information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Provided by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm showing this page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Misic, we can see that on this document of the ICMP concerning missing persons, the reviewers are, among others, Ewa Tabeau and Christian Jennings. Do you have any information in which way was Ewa Tabeau involved in the work of the ICMP and which data she used?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last topic we shall discuss relates to one document I want to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just as a reminder, we should not broadcast it. Just a moment, please. So the document we need is D1096. Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't mention the name, because you know what this is about. Did your institute follow the ICMP's method of work in analysing DNA?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we are not able to follow that, nor is it part our purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone from the officialdom of Republika Srpska participated in the DNA analysis procedures?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the personnel of the ICMP's DNA laboratories. I don't know who works there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And regarding the mortal remains you were asked about, you said you could not rule out the possibility they were found at Snagovo. Can you confirm that these mortal remains were found there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm. I can only suppose somebody brought them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness had answered that question previously. It was perfectly clear that the witness didn't know anything about it and that therefore he couldn't exclude it and that, of course, implicitly says that he can't confirm it. And now the witness says that you only can suppose somebody brought them there. Can you also suppose that they were buried there without being brought by any third party, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It sounds very unlikely. I could hardly believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but those were all the questions I had for Mr. Misic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then there is nothing to proceed any further, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just thank Mr. Misic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- if you -- with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that. Mr. Jeremy, any further questions for Mr. Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, no, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, this then concludes your evidence given in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench, and I would wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy, if you open the door, perhaps there is a witness waiting behind it and could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll see to it, Your Honours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tusevljak. Please be seated. Mr. Tusevljak, you'll first be examined by Mr. Sasa Lukic. Mr. Lukic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic. MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you, Your Honour. Examination by Mr. S. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to slowly, for the record, state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Simo Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The 12th of February, 1965, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete secondary school and elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Upon completing secondary school, did you go to university?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the faculty of security in Skopje in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I enrolled in 1984 and I graduated in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get a job after graduation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as I graduated from university I got a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak more slowly, please, for the record, so that everything that you are saying in response to my questions can be transcribed. Where did you get this job after university?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The secretariat of the interior, the municipal SUP, Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which duty did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Inspector for general crime at the municipal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I remained in that position for a year and a half, and after that I was transferred to the city SUP of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which duties did you perform then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Co-ordinator for property-related crime in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many police stations are there in the city of Sarajevo or were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At that time there were ten public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many municipalities were there in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Ten urban municipalities. And each and every one of them had its own public security station. And they were within the city SUP of Sarajevo, the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how it is decided what the number of policemen in a particular police station will be.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The number of policemen was determined on the basis of the number of inhabitants: 1 policeman per 1.000 inhabitants. So that is how the number of authorised officers in the public security station would be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time was there a reserve police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In the public security stations, there was also a reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to tell us how the number of reserve policemen was determined for a particular public security station.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, at the time there were two times more of them than there were active duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that always the case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: All the way up until 1990, when the number of reserve policemen started increasing abruptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was there this abrupt increase in the number of reserve policemen; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: After the multiparty elections in 1990, 1991, the number of reserve policemen was increased because the reserve police also became the party police, to a certain extent, of the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did these people come from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In most cases, these people were not citizens of Sarajevo. They were not local people from Sarajevo. They came from Sandzak. That is a part of Serbia, a region in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which part of Serbia is Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Sandzak is in the southern part of Serbia. It's on the border between Serbia and Montenegro, and it was in both republics. In fact, it separates Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people who came from Sandzak to Sarajevo, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: They were all ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how they declare themselves today?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Today they declare themselves as Bosniaks. In 1990, that ethnicity did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who it was that brought them there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: They were brought there by the Party of Democratic Action. They were brought to these police positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know which structures they were recruited from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, they were recruited from rural areas, from their own party structures, and these persons were not professional policemen. They became policemen only in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which milieu they would come?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, that was the first time that persons who were prone to crime joined the police force, although that was prohibited by law. These were persons that we had processed on account of crimes, and they were given official IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the necessary requirements for a person to become a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At that time in accordance with the law, there were general requirements and special requirements. The general requirements were that you had to have a secondary school education, that you should be fit and healthy, and not have a criminal record. As for special prerequisites, for certain specialities certain skills and knowledge were required so that you could become an active duty policeman. You'd have to complete the secondary police school in the neighbourhood of Vrace in Sarajevo, or you'd have to complete a six-month course for a policeman that was also organised in the secondary school at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, who kept criminal records?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The public security stations or the city SUP for the ten municipalities of Sarajevo. According to the law, criminal records were kept at one's place of birth in the former Yugoslavia. So it depended on where you were born. If you had a criminal record, it would be kept at your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these persons that you told us about just now, did you notice that there were some other formations in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Already in the beginning of 1991, there were paramilitary formations of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the founder of these units?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Also the Party of Democratic Action and certain former officers of the JNA, as well as some of the top officials in the then Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were some of your colleagues among them, people you knew personally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. People I knew personally who worked either at public security stations or at the city SUP, the centre of public security of Sarajevo, and the MUP of the RBiH; that is to say, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you know how these persons were being armed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Already in 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was illegal arming. In certain police operations that I personally took part in, we would uncover such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I personally, in co-operation with the police, was once in a position to stop a van where there were 400 snipers, and it was evident that this was arms smuggling because the van was owned by the Islamic community, the Islamic religious community in Sarajevo, and the documentation said that it was for the hunting society of Citluk in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is well known that already then there was a war raging in Croatia. There was this other case too when the police station of Hadzici stopped a truck full of weapons and the police brought them to the police station in Hadzici, and the then chief of the public security station of Sarajevo - I cannot recall his name this very instant - the truck was allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I can give you some other examples from that period --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. S. LUKIC: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your last answer, because the last part of your sentence is not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I said -- can I start from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: On one occasion we stopped a van that was owned by the Islamic religious community, and in that van there were 400 snipers. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All that is on the record, only the last part was missing. There is no need to repeat everything, only the last part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I can tell you about the Hadzici police station, where the police stopped a truck full of weapons and ammunition and on orders from the then chief of the public security police station was allowed to leave; although, this was an obvious case of arms smuggling for the Party of Democratic Action. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find -- MR. S. LUKIC: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to get some clarification. How big was this van, sir? Obviously smaller than a truck. You have used words "van" and "truck."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first case, it was a van. A Volkswagon. And then there is also Renault and Fiats and these are smaller vehicles that are used for transporting smaller quantities. They can transport up to 1.000 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stop that. I'm not talking about that. I am just talking about the one van. Okay. You say it was a Kombi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it could carry 400 people or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not people, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the record said "snipers," it didn't say "sniper rifles," so I thought you were talking about people. I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed. MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you told us that you investigated a case - that is to say, the transportation of these 400 sniper rifles - can you explain to us what the rules were regarding the transportation of such quantities of weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The rule is that the Ministry of the Interior should be informed about that, and they provide a permit or approval for this kind of transportation and also they provide a police escort from the place where the weapons are loaded to the place where they were unloaded. Of course, the transport is checked whether it is legal and whether the persons involved in the transportation have permits from appropriate state authorities for this kind of trade, for this kind of transport, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that transport have that sort of escort, and was the transport of these rifles announced to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, if it had been approved, we would have responded appropriately. This was discovered quite by chance by a police inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina was Alija Delimustafic, and his deputy in charge of the police was Avdo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they professional policemen? Excuse me, let me just interrupt you. Could you repeat the deputy's name.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the deputies for police and his counsellors. It was Avdo Hebib.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they professional policemen? Did they have police training?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The minister of the interior was a political figure, nominated by the SDA party. And out of all police training, he had completed a secondary school for the police. So it was rather low-level police training. And if he had not been a political nominee, he would have never met the requirements for the job of the minister of interior. And Avdo Hebib was a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in Sarajevo at the time? I mean the political situation; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At that time, the tensions in Sarajevo were running very high, and interethnic relations were strained to the maximum. The incidents of crime was very high, and the number of crimes recorded per day was on the rise constantly. There were even some areas of Sarajevo, which is a relatively small city, 400.000 population, where you had 20 to 30 crimes per day; robberies, forced confiscations of cars, break-ins. All forms of crime. The situation was getting worse and worse by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the police depots holding weapons and ammunition at risk?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, they were not at risk because the police was well-trained and equipped and quite able to secure every depot in the city of Sarajevo properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the weapons and ammunition from police depots were transferred to other depots in the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: What I know is that as the number of reserve policemen increased, reserve policemen were being issued long-barrel weapons, and more and more rifles ended up in the hands of reserve policemen who kept them at their homes. So a lot of weapons were drawn from the depots and distributed to certain groups within the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that these weapons were also used to arm the population that was coming in from Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Absolutely. And everyone who was being inducted into the reserve force of the police. MR. S. LUKIC: Can we see now 65 ter 1D0479 [sic], first page both in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just mention, I notice that you're asking a number of leading questions. Can you be careful to make sure that your questions are not leading. An example is: "Does it mean that these weapons were also used to arm the population that was coming from Sandzak?" You're just telling him the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it also causes -- MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that we don't have any clue as to why the witness knows that, and that's, of course, a result of the way of questioning the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you repeat the number, please. MR. S. LUKIC: 1D05479. We can see it now on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off. MR. S. LUKIC: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was able to take the decision to transfer weapons from one place to another?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Only the minister of the interior and whoever was in charge of those weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the chef de cabinet of the minister of the interior able to take such a decision?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, he didn't have those powers. He didn't have powers relating to anything that had to do with weapons. There were deputies in charge of the police force, deputies of the minister who were able to take such decisions and issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If there were a written order from the minister of the interior, would the chef de cabinet then be able to decide to remove weapons from one depot to another?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, it had to go directly through the minister. And at a meeting of the collegium, the minister would have to take that decision. Because if you are moving weapons from one depot to another, the police from that area had to secure the transport and to escort it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see a document before you. Tell me, who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The chef de cabinet, Mesud Omerspahic. At the time he was head of the minister's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see from this document that the weapons were moved from the Rakovica installation to the Zlatiste installation. Was there some security risk hanging over the Rakovica installation where the weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a little reminder. That's actually not what the document says. So to avoid any misstatements of the evidence, perhaps we could just stick to what's on the face of the document. The document reflects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That they were to be moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know whether it's a translation issue or not, but the translation says that you had told the witness that this order -- the document says that the weapons were moved, whereas the document says that they are to be moved. MR. S. LUKIC: Yes, that's right, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's evident from the document, and it's my mistake that I misspoke, that the weapons were to be moved from one installation to another. So let me rephrase this question. Was there a security risk for the Rakovica installation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Rakovica was a special-purpose depot of the Ministry of the Interior, the security services centre of Sarajevo. And there was police equipment secured by police details. I was in Sarajevo at the time and I know it well, about the security situation there, and I can say confidently there was not the slightest security risk to police depot or this police equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was held in the Zlatiste depot at the time? At the Zlatiste installation.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Zlatiste was, on the surface, a hotel or a restaurant. And below, there were depots and warehouses holding, for the most part, the archives, case files, and the documentation from the previous period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. Would this be a suitable moment? MR. S. LUKIC: Yes, it is. But I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please -- MR. S. LUKIC: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put that one question to the witness, and we'll take the break after we've heard his answer. MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that type of building meet all the requirements for holding weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: From what I know, it doesn't. I went inside after the war. And from what I saw, it was not made to hold weapons and ammunition and it was not used for that purpose before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break now. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
